issues.issue: The parenthetical defining B-4 Partners LLC is garbled ("(“Managers Fund and Manager each being referred to mdividually as a “Borrower”"), so the label attached to the second party is not cleanly stated. The joint-and-several designation is otherwise plain.

"Control" is defined as the power to direct management and policies "whether through the ownership of Stock, by contract, or otherwise," a general catch-all sitting against two enumerated means. The 10%/director/joint-venture deeming rules are then switched on only "for purposes of the definition of Eligible Notes Receivable and Section 7.13," leaving the term with two different reaches in the same instrument.

The definition closes with "together with any obligations undertaken or assumed relating thereto," an open-ended catch-all appended to two specifically described obligations of the Fund. What else counts as "relating thereto" is not bounded.

The three alternatives run from a FIRREA-compliant appraisal to anything "otherwise acceptable to Lender" to "an informal or unwritten estimate of value by Servicer," so the term has no fixed content. A dispute over what qualifies as an "Authorized Appraisal" would turn on which limb governs.

"Bank Product" is "any financial accommodation extended ... by a Bank Product Provider (other than pursuant to this Agreement) including" seven listed services, leaving the general phrase's reach against the specific list uncertain. Because Bank Product Obligations are secured, the boundary matters.

The definition makes "a Borrower" mean "each of and either of Fund and Manager," while Section 1.2 provides that in any financial covenant "Borrower" means Fund and its Subsidiaries on a consolidated basis. Which sense governs a given covenant is not always evident.

The grant is over "all property, including, without limitation, each of the following," but the twelve enumerated categories omit Real Property and Real Estate Owned even though clause (l) mentions Real Property only as proceeds. A court could be asked whether the general words or the enumerated list fixes the collateral pool.

The term is defined wholly by reference to an unattached extrinsic document, "the written policies, procedures and guidelines of Fund ... in the form delivered to Lender and approved by Lender prior to the Closing Date." Since eligibility, extensions and appraisals all turn on it, its content is contestable outside the four corners.

"Collections" means "all cash, checks, notes, instruments, and other items of payment," with an inclusion list (insurance proceeds, proceeds of cash sales, rental proceeds, tax refunds) that says nothing about proceeds of a sale or payoff of a Note Receivable. Whether such proceeds are "Collections" is left open by the general-versus-specific structure.

Section 2.6(a) separately requires payoff and sale proceeds of Notes Receivable to be routed to a Cash Management Account, which suggests those proceeds are not already captured by "Collections" in clause (ii) of that same subsection. The two readings of "Collections" cannot both be right.

A Note Receivable is "Defaulted" if "Administrative Borrower or Lender deems" it non-performing or non-collectible, an undefined and purely subjective standard exercisable by either side. Nothing states what happens when the two disagree.

The exclusion criteria "may be modified from time to time by Lender in Lender's Permitted Discretion" and every exclusion is subject to the Lender's case-by-case override, so the class is defined by unilateral determination rather than by the listed criteria. The interaction of the twenty-one exclusions with clauses (t) and (u), which are applied to a separately computed "Preliminary Eligible Notes Receivable," adds a further layer of contestable mechanics.

Clause (a) sweeps in "any other formulation intended to define, list, or classify substances by reason of deleterious properties," a general catch-all after four enumerated statutory labels. Its reach beyond the listed categories is not fixed.

Clause (d) makes "all obligations or liabilities of others secured by a Lien on any asset of a Person" that Person's own Indebtedness "irrespective of whether such obligation or liability is assumed," which is far broader than the other enumerated categories. Whether that clause counts non-recourse third-party debt against the Section 7.1 covenant is contestable.

The definition is circular and self-referential: an Investor Membership Interest is "an interest in a member's interest in Fund issued or to be issued by Fund pursuant to an Offering Circular." Whether it means the member's own equity interest or a derivative interest in it is genuinely unclear.

Section 9.1(e) and 9.1(o) charge amounts to Borrowers as "Lender Group Expenses," a term the Agreement never defines; only "Lender Expenses" is defined here. Whether the Section 9.1 amounts fall within this definition has to be worked out.

The definition sweeps in "leases, and other title exceptions and encumbrances affecting Real Property," so ordinary easements and leases are "Liens" for purposes of the Section 7.2 blanket prohibition. Permitted Liens clause (k) excuses easements only for Real Property, leaving other title exceptions technically prohibited.

After a closed list of named documents, the definition adds "any other agreement entered into, now or in the future, by any Borrower and Lender in connection with this Agreement." How far that general catch-all reaches beyond the enumerated instruments is left open, and defaults under "Loan Documents" are Events of Default.

"Material adverse change in the business, prospects, operations, results of operations, assets, liabilities or financial condition" turns on the undefined words "material" and, notably, "prospects," with no baseline or threshold given. The term gates Section 3.3(d) advances and Section 8.9, so its boundary is squarely operative.

A $50,000,000 facility cannot be drawn without breaching Section 7.16(b), which caps the Senior Leverage Ratio (Obligations over Tangible Net Worth) at 0.9% while Section 7.16(a) sets minimum Tangible Net Worth at $600,000,000 — a ceiling of roughly $5.4 million of Obligations. The stated commitment and the financial covenant cannot both be given effect.

The parenthetical "(less portions that are not in compliance with the definition thereof)" subtracts from an aggregate that, by definition, already excludes non-complying notes. Whether it is surplusage or a second haircut is unclear.

The definition dates the test from "after the Effective Date," but "Effective Date" is not a defined term anywhere in this Agreement, which uses "Closing Date" throughout (including in the parallel carve-out in the "Subsidiary" definition). The date from which an entity qualifies as a New Fund is therefore unfixed.

The definition requires a Lien on "real property owned by the maker of such note," which by its terms excludes any loan secured by property owned by a third party or an affiliate of the maker. Whether such loans are Notes Receivable at all — and so part of the collateral and Borrowing Base — is contestable.

"A determination made in the exercise of reasonable (from the perspective of a secured asset-based lender) business judgment" fuses an objective reasonableness test with a partisan point of view, and gives no benchmark. Nearly every discretionary Lender act in the Agreement is measured by it.

Clause (c) permits "the use or transfer of money or Cash Equivalents in a manner that is not prohibited by the terms of this Agreement" — a circular catch-all sitting alongside six tightly specified dispositions, so its reach is set only by whatever else the Agreement happens not to forbid. Clause (e) compounds this by permitting sales of Notes Receivable "for a cash purchase price of not less than eighty (80%) of the unpaid balance," a figure whose unit is left out.

Section 4.1 states that "except for Permitted Dispositions, Borrowers and their Subsidiaries shall have no authority, express or implied, to dispose of any item or portion of the Collateral," and Sections 7.3(c) and 7.4 rest on the same carve-out. A broad reading of this definition would swallow those prohibitions and let the Borrowers release collateral at will.

Clause (c) reads "so long as such Liens for Approved Debt or subordinated to the Liens held by Lender on the terms approved by Lender" — the word "are" is missing, so the condition on which Approved Debt liens qualify as Permitted Liens is grammatically incoherent. Clause (e) also refers to Liens securing "Purchase Money Indebtedness" and then conditions them on securing "Permitted Purchase Money Indebtedness."

Condition (a) requires the reorganization to be "consistent in all material respects with the written description provided to Lender by Borrowers prior to the Closing Date," an extrinsic document neither attached nor described. What the Permitted Reorganization actually authorises therefore cannot be determined from the instrument.

Real Estate Owned is treated throughout as collateral — it is listed on the Borrowing Base Certificate and its sale is a Permitted Disposition — yet the "Borrower Collateral" definition does not enumerate Real Property among the granted categories. The two provisions leave the status of foreclosed real estate unsettled.

Clause (d) defines a Restricted Payment as a payment on Subordinated Debt or holder Indebtedness "to the extent such action would cause an Event of Default to occur hereunder," which is circular because Section 7.10's prohibition on Restricted Payments is itself what creates the Event of Default. Clause (e) then adds a residual for any payment "not expressly authorized in this Agreement."

The ratio is Obligations over Tangible Net Worth, and Section 7.16(b) caps it at 0.9% "expressed as a percentage"; with the $600,000,000 minimum Tangible Net Worth required by Section 7.16(a), that permits only about $5.4 million of Obligations against a $50,000,000 Maximum Revolver Amount. The definition and the covenant cannot be harmonised with the facility size.

"Solvent" is given a bare balance-sheet meaning — "at fair valuations, the sum of such Person's assets is greater than all of such Person's debts" — with no definition of "debts" (contingent, disputed, subordinated?) and none of the customary capital-adequacy or ability-to-pay prongs. Since Section 5.12 is captioned "Fraudulent Transfer," the gap between this test and the statutory ones is exactly what a court would have to construe.

Clause (a) requires Subordinated Debt to be "unsecured Indebtedness," yet clause (b) brings in Approved Debt, which the "Subordinated Note" definition says is "secured by the assets of Fund" and which Schedule P-1 lists as a Permitted Lien. The definition therefore both requires and does not require the debt to be unsecured.

A Subordinated Note is said to be "secured by the assets of Fund," while the "Subordinated Debt" definition, clause (a), requires such debt to be "unsecured Indebtedness." The two definitions of the same layer of debt point in opposite directions.

The carve-outs mean that an entity formed after the Closing Date, any New Fund, and Bar-K, Inc. are not "Subsidiaries," yet Section 7.13 forbids Borrowers to "form or acquire any Subsidiary without the prior written consent of Lender" and the Change of Control definition turns on control of Subsidiaries. The covenant can be sidestepped by the very entities the definition excludes.

The formula adds "Subordinated Debt" to members' equity in computing Tangible Net Worth, so borrowed money counts toward net worth, and the connector between limbs (a) and (b) is rendered "tins" rather than "minus." What the covenant actually measures is open to argument.

The definition speaks of distributions by "Fund or Manager" but then measures them by taxes attributable to the income "of such Borrower," a phrase with no antecedent in the sentence. Whose income sets the ceiling is unclear.

Section 2.1(b) makes the occurrence of a Triggering Event the sole gateway to Lender-imposed reserves, but Section 10 lets Lender "set up such reserves against the Borrowing Base or the Maximum Revolver Amount as Lender deems necessary" whenever a Borrower fails to pay third-party monies, with no Triggering Event required. The trigger is therefore not the limit it purports to be.

The direction that "Borrower" in a financial covenant means "Fund and its Subsidiaries on a consolidated basis unless the context clearly requires otherwise" sits against the "Borrower" definition, which makes it "each of and either of Fund and Manager." Which sense applies to the Senior Leverage Ratio, computed on "Obligations of Borrower," is left to context.

The subsection first gives Lender an unrestricted right to establish reserves "in such amounts, and with respect to such matters, as Lender in its Permitted Discretion shall deem necessary," then promises "not to establish any such reserves unless a Triggering Event has occurred and is continuing." Section 10 independently authorises reserves against the Borrowing Base with no Triggering Event, so the restriction cannot be given full effect.

The second limit is expressed as a compound test — the Maximum Revolver Amount less Revolver Usage plus cash in the Cash Management Accounts may not exceed "the aggregate amount of unfunded commitments of Fund to the makers of Notes Receivable" — which reverses the usual direction of a borrowing limit and is not otherwise explained. Its practical operation is genuinely obscure.

The waterfall applies to "all such payments, and all proceeds of Collateral received by Lender," while Section 2.6(b)(iii) requires the Cash Management Banks to sweep all account balances to the Lender's Account daily whether or not any Obligation is then due. Whether ordinary daily sweeps are applied through this waterfall or merely credited under Section 2.7 is not resolved.

The default rate is fixed at four points "above the per annum rate otherwise applicable to Base Rate Loans," so a LIBOR Rate Loan in default is repriced off a rate that was not "otherwise applicable" to it. Which rate a defaulted LIBOR advance bears is arguable.

Clause (ii) requires deposit of "all of their Collections" into an account "in Fund's name," while clause (iii) separately requires sale and payoff proceeds of Notes Receivable to be remitted by the escrow or title company to a Cash Management Account — leaving it uncertain whether such proceeds are "Collections" and what happens to Manager's own receipts in an account held only in Fund's name. The obligations are cast on the Borrowers but the operative money movement depends on third parties.

The closing sentence provides that from 60 days after the Closing Date "Wells Fargo shall be the only Cash Management Bank and all of the Cash Management Accounts shall be maintained at Wells Fargo," which cannot be squared with Section 2.6(c), permitting Administrative Borrower to amend Schedule 2.6 to add or replace Cash Management Banks, or with Schedule 2.6, which names Greater Bay Bank and The Mechanics Bank.

The subsection purports to impose the primary obligation on non-parties — "Each Cash Management Bank shall establish and maintain Cash Management Agreements with Lender and each Borrower" — without saying that the Borrowers must procure it, so whose breach a failure is remains open. The required term (iii), a daily sweep of "all amounts in the applicable Cash Management Account," is likewise stated as the bank's undertaking rather than the Borrowers'.

Section 2.6(e) applies the same Cash Management Agreement machinery to Escrow Accounts but expressly permits Borrower "to withdraw funds from the Escrow Accounts on a daily basis" to fund escrow draws, which cannot stand with this subsection's requirement that the bank sweep all amounts to the Lender's Account daily. The two provisions direct the same dollars to different places.

This subsection lets Administrative Borrower amend Schedule 2.6 to add or replace Cash Management Banks with Lender's consent, while Section 2.6(a) provides that after 60 days "Wells Fargo shall be the only Cash Management Bank." The permission and the prohibition overlap without a stated ordering.

Borrower is "permitted to withdraw funds from the Escrow Accounts on a daily basis" to fund escrow draws, but Section 2.6(b)(iii) requires each Cash Management Agreement to provide for a daily sweep of all amounts in the account to the Lender's Account. Escrow funds cannot both be swept and remain available for draws.

The sentence reads "Administrative Borrower agrees to establish establish and maintain the Designated Account," and the authority to advance without instructions is keyed to "Section 2.5(c)," a payment-charging provision rather than an advance provision. The cross-reference does not do the work the sentence assumes.
The fee is described as "a monthly loan administration equal to $2,000" — the noun "fee" is missing from the operative phrase. The omission is trivial in practice but leaves the charge unnamed.

The unused line fee is stated as "one-half of one percent (0.30%) per annum": the words and the numeral in parentheses give two different rates. A court asked to fix the fee would have to choose between them.

The payment deadline reads "payable within $0 days after presentation by Lender of a statement," so the notice period is not legible from the text. When the increased-cost payment falls due cannot be determined.

This subsection converts a LIBOR Rate Loan to the Base Rate at the end of each Interest Period "unless Administrative Borrower properly has exercised the LIBOR Option," whereas Section 2.12(c) deems Borrower to have elected the LIBOR Option for every Interest Period unless it affirmatively opts for the Base Rate. The default position on rollover is stated twice, in opposite terms.

The deemed ongoing LIBOR election here is the mirror image of Section 2.12(a), which provides that the rate "automatically shall convert" to the Base Rate at the end of an Interest Period unless the LIBOR Option has been properly exercised. Absent any notice from Borrower, the two subsections produce different rates.

The subsection fixes obligations "under the provisions of this Section 2,15," but there is no Section 2.15 in the Agreement; the intended reference is Section 2.13. The clause that defines the scope of each Borrower's absolute liability points to nothing.

The waiver is framed entirely by reference to "Section 580(d) of the California Code of Civil Procedure," while Section 13(a) provides that the Agreement is governed and construed under New York law. Whether a New York-governed waiver of California antideficiency defenses operates as written is a live question.

Sub-clause (ii)(B) confers rights on "Agent and Lenders" — "Agent" is not a party to or defined term in this bilateral agreement, and "Lender" is singular throughout. The waiver is expressed in favour of persons who do not exist under this instrument.

The premium is imposed on any early termination "for any reason not set forth in Section 3.7(a)," including acceleration on default and sale of Collateral in an Insolvency Proceeding, and is justified by a recital of "impracticability and extreme difficulty of ascertaining the actual amount of damages." Whether that stipulation makes the charge enforceable liquidated damages rather than a penalty is the classic dispute this wording invites.

The grant reaches only "Borrower Collateral," whose definition enumerates no Real Property, yet Section 4.4(c) requires documents "to create and perfect Liens in favor of Lender in any owned Real Property acquired after the Closing Date" and Permitted Dispositions (g) contemplates releasing Real Estate Owned. Whether the granting clause itself reaches real property is unsettled.

The sequence is circular: Lender must return the note "when a Note Receivable ... is repaid in its entirety" but returns it "to facilitate its payment," and releases its Lien "promptly upon receipt of the final payment." Whether the note goes back before or after payoff is the very thing the sentence needs to settle.

The release duty is triggered when a note is "sold by Fund in accordance with the terms of this Agreement," which routes back through the Permitted Dispositions definition and its 80%-of-unpaid-balance sale limb. The content of the release obligation is only as determinate as that carve-out.

The representation measures the Borrowers' loan documents against forms "commensurate with forms and documentation used by prudent lenders in the same or similar circumstances," a benchmark that is nowhere defined. The sentence also makes the absolute claim that "all aspects of Borrowers' operations, comply with all applicable federal, state and local laws and regulations."

The representation qualifies itself by reference to what is "described on Schedule 5.8 or in an Offering Circular," but no Offering Circular is attached to or identified in the Agreement. The exception is measured by a document outside the instrument.

The representation that "the Lender's Liens are validly created, perfected, and first priority Liens, subject only to Permitted Liens" is hard to reconcile with the Permitted Liens definition and Section 2.1(b), which contemplate existing Schedule P-1 liens "specifically identified thereon as entitled to have priority over the Lender's Liens." First priority and permitted senior liens cannot both hold.

This representation, captioned "Fraudulent Transfer," rests entirely on the defined term "Solvent," which the Agreement reduces to a bare balance-sheet comparison of assets and debts. The caption and the defined test do not measure the same thing.

The representation is qualified three times by "(taken as a whole)" and then requires that the information not be "incomplete by omitting to state any fact necessary to make such information (taken as a whole) not misleading." Whether a specific false statement is cured by the aggregate is exactly what the qualifier leaves open.

After a detailed schedule of dated deliverables, item (h) requires "such other reports as to the Collateral or the financial condition of each Borrower and its Subsidiaries, as Lender may request" — an open catch-all whose reach against the enumerated items is undefined, and breach of Section 6.2 is an immediate Event of Default under Section 8.2(a).

The collection covenant is circular — "use commercially reasonable efforts ... to promptly and diligently collect and enforce payment of all Notes Receivable to the extent that it is commercially reasonable to do so and in a commercially reasonable manner" — so the standard measures itself. No benchmark for adequate collection effort is supplied.

Borrowers must deliver policies "with an endorsement naming Lender as the sole loss payee (under a satisfactory lender's loss payable endorsement) or additional insured, as appropriate" — the choice between the two, and who decides what is "appropriate," is not stated. The difference matters to who controls proceeds under Section 6.8(b).

The enumerated separateness covenants run "(a) ... (c) ... and (d)" with no clause (b), so one item of the list the parties evidently agreed on is missing from the operative text. Whether an unstated separateness undertaking binds the Borrowers is left unresolved by the face of the section.

The covenant applies only "to the extent necessary to comply with Section 4.2," which requires delivery of enough notes to keep $250,000,000 of Eligible Notes Receivable with Lender, whereas the Eligible Notes Receivable definition, clauses (r) and (s), conditions eligibility of every note on delivery and recorded assignment. The delivery duty is therefore stated at two different scopes.

This covenant requires escrowed amounts to be deposited into "a Deposit Account that is subject to a perfected Lender's Lien," while Section 2.6(e) requires the same funds to be held in an Escrow Account at a Cash Management Bank under a Cash Management Agreement. The two locations for the same money are stated independently.

The covenant requires escrow instructions that call for "delivery by such maker of each of the documents listed in Section 3.3(z)," but Section 3.3 has only subsections (a) through (f) and contains no clause (z); the documents intended are those in Section 3.1(t). The disbursement condition points to a subsection that does not exist.

Section 7.4 bars any disposal of assets other than Permitted Dispositions, while Section 7.3(c) bars only the disposal of "all or any substantial part of its assets" other than Permitted Dispositions. Two overlapping prohibitions of different reach cover the same conduct.

The covenant forbids material changes to Borrower's Required Procedures "without advance notice to, and consent by, the Lender" but fixes no notice period, and "in any material respect" is left unmeasured. Compare the definition of Borrower's Required Procedures, which requires prior written approval in Lender's sole discretion.

The carve-out permits Fund to "make distributions to holders of Investor Membership Interests for the return of capital to the extent required or permitted by Fund's Governing Documents," handing the measure of the exception to an extrinsic document that the Lender does not control. How large a hole that leaves in the Restricted Payments prohibition cannot be read off the Agreement.

Section 8.9(x) makes a default in "capital obligations to any member or former member in connection with their Investor Membership Interests" an Event of Default, while this section allows those very distributions only when no Default has occurred or would result. The two provisions push in opposite directions once redemptions come under strain.

After two specific prohibitions — transfers of property to an Affiliate (a) and acquisitions of Notes Receivable from an Affiliate (b) — clause (c) sweeps in "any other transaction between such Borrower and any Affiliate," subject only to four soft conditions ("ordinary course," "fair and reasonable terms," "fully disclosed," "no less favorable ... than ... arm's length"). The reach of that general catch-all against the enumerated specifics, and the expanded 10% "Affiliate" test that applies only for this Section, are both open to argument.

The whole section is prefaced "Except for Permitted Dispositions and Permitted Investments," and Permitted Dispositions clause (e) allows any sale of a Note Receivable at 80% of the unpaid balance without limiting the buyer, so property may be moved to an Affiliate through the very carve-out clause (a) purports to prohibit. The prohibition and the carve-out cannot both be given full effect.

Proceeds may be used for "funding of its obligations with respect to any Investor Membership Interests or pursuant to a Permitted Reorganization," a phrase that is undefined and would on its face cover using advances to cash out withdrawing members. What counts as such an "obligation" is the whole question.

Section 7.10 prohibits Restricted Payments, which by definition include distributions and redemption payments on Stock in a Borrower, yet this section authorises the use of Advance proceeds for obligations relating to Investor Membership Interests. The permitted use and the payment prohibition overlap without a stated priority.

Subsection (b) caps the Senior Leverage Ratio — Obligations divided by Tangible Net Worth — at 0.9%, which together with subsection (a)'s $600,000,000 minimum Tangible Net Worth allows only about $5.4 million of Obligations, against the $50,000,000 Maximum Revolver Amount committed by Section 2.1(a). Read literally, drawing the facility breaches the covenant from the outset.

Section 8.9(x) makes an Event of Default out of a default in "its capital obligations to any member or former member in connection with their Investor Membership Interests," a category the Agreement nowhere defines, and clause (z) is a general catch-all for "any other agreement" following two specific ones. Section 8.3 similarly turns on whether "any material portion" of assets "comes into the possession of any third Person."

Clauses (e) and (o) provide that amounts Lender incurs "shall be Lender Group Expenses," a term the Agreement never defines; the defined term is "Lender Expenses." Whether those amounts are recoverable Obligations at all turns on a phrase with no referent.

This section lets Lender, "in its sole discretion and without prior notice," set up reserves against the Borrowing Base or the Maximum Revolver Amount whenever a Borrower fails to pay third-party monies, which contradicts Section 2.1(b)'s express agreement "not to establish any such reserves unless a Triggering Event has occurred and is continuing." Both cannot govern the same reserve.

The indemnity is expressly extended to liabilities "WHICH IN WHOLE OR IN PART ARE CAUSED BY OR ARISE OUT OF ANY NEGLIGENT ACT OR OMISSION OF SUCH INDEMNIFIED PERSON," while the closing proviso excludes liabilities "resulting from the gross negligence or willful misconduct." Where a loss is caused partly by ordinary and partly by gross negligence, the two sentences point in different directions.

New York law is chosen for construction and enforcement, yet Sections 2.13(g) and 2.13(h) frame the Borrowers' waivers entirely in terms of Sections 580a, 580b, 580d and 726 of the California Code of Civil Procedure. Which body of law supplies the antideficiency rules being waived is not resolved.

Actions "shall be tried and litigated only in" New York County courts, but the proviso lets Lender bring any suit seeking enforcement against Collateral "in the courts of any jurisdiction where Lender elects." The clause is exclusive against the Borrowers and permissive for the Lender, and how far the "enforcement against Collateral" carve-out reaches is undefined.

The subsection restricts assignments to "Eligible Transferees" in minimum $5,000,000 amounts, then provides that "the Assignee need not be an Eligible Transferee if such assignment is in connection with any merger, consolidation, sale, transfer, or other disposition of all or any substantial portion of the business or loan portfolio" of the Lender. The exception is broad enough to consume the rule.

"Unless the contrary is compelled by the context, everything contained in each Section applies equally to this entire Agreement" is an instruction of uncertain content, apparently meaning the opposite of the headings-only disclaimer that precedes it. What it directs a reader to do with a section-specific term is genuinely obscure.

The section disclaims construction of "any uncertainty or ambiguity herein ... against Lender or Borrowers," removing contra proferentem, and then directs interpretation "according to the ordinary meaning of the words used so as to accomplish fairly the purposes and intentions of all parties." Whether that displaces the ordinary rule against the drafter is itself a question of construction.

The section directs that in the event of a required withholding "Borrowers shall comply with the penultimate sentence of this Section 16.5," but the penultimate sentence of the section is the gross-up proviso, not a compliance direction. The internal pointer does not land where the sentence assumes.

The integration clause says the Loan Documents "shall not be contradicted or qualified by any other agreement, oral or written, before the date hereof," yet the Agreement's operative content depends on pre-closing extrinsic documents — Borrower's Required Procedures and the "written description provided to Lender by Borrowers prior to the Closing Date" in the Permitted Reorganization definition. Whether those documents are excluded or incorporated is unresolved.

Paragraph 5 repeats the representation already given in paragraph 2 of the same certificate but with a different exception formula — "except as set forth on Schedule 2" rather than the earlier carve-out for matters "permitted by Lender." The certificate makes the same statement twice on inconsistent terms.

The certification is of compliance with "Sections 7.16, and 7.37 of the Loan Agreement," but there is no Section 7.37; the covenant intended is Section 7.17. The certificate therefore certifies compliance with a provision that does not exist.

The Designated Account is identified as a Greater Bay Bank account in B-4 Partners' name, while Section 2.6(a) requires that from 60 days after the Closing Date "Wells Fargo shall be the only Cash Management Bank and all of the Cash Management Accounts shall be maintained at Wells Fargo." Whether the Designated Account survives that migration is not addressed.

Item 2 admits "the Subordinated Liens securing Approved Debt" as Permitted Liens once a Permitted Reorganization is implemented, while the "Subordinated Debt" definition, clause (a), describes such debt as "unsecured Indebtedness." The schedule contemplates security that the definition denies.

The schedule discloses an established practice of redeeming members' Interests and 50 pending redemption requests, whereas Section 7.10 prohibits Restricted Payments — which by definition include any "redemption, retirement, sinking fund or similar payment, purchase or other acquisition for value ... of any class of Stock in a Borrower" — except within narrow carve-outs. The disclosure and the operative covenant describe different regimes.
